stances.claim: The constitutional text and framers' intent — supported by the Bernas-Rodrigo-Monsod exchanges in the 1986 ConCom — require Congress to convene in joint session to deliberate and vote as a single body, not merely when revoking but when reviewing ML; the two chambers' separate sessions in May 2017 were less than faithful to this mandate.
stances.rhetorical_move: textual-plus-intent argument using framer testimony as co-evidence for joint-session requirement
stances.confidence: asserted as probable correct reading, without condemning Congress

stances.claim: The Fortun vs Arroyo pronouncements on Congress's 'automatic' duty to convene jointly are obiter dictum — not binding ratio decidendi — because the petition was dismissed as moot when GMA lifted ML before the Court could rule; future ML challenges cannot rely on Fortun as precedent for this point.
stances.rhetorical_move: obiter-vs-ratio distinction as a precedent-reliability check

stances.claim: The Court should issue a definitive ruling on the joint-session requirement now — for prospective guidance — but need not issue a writ of mandamus compelling Congress, extending the benefit of good faith given the prior ambiguity from Fortun's obiter status.
stances.rhetorical_move: split-remedy recommendation: rule on the constitutional question without the coercive writ
stances.confidence: recommended as the prudent middle path

notable_anecdotes: Christian Monsod being both a drafter of the 1986 Constitutional Commission provision on congressional ML review and a current petitioner in the Hilbay mandamus group — the same person defending the framers' intent he helped write, an unusual convergence of constitutional authorship and litigant advocacy.

CJ's disclosure that Fortun's 'automatic' joint-session language — cited extensively by the petitioners — is merely obiter because GMA lifted ML before the Court could rule, effectively stripping what appeared to be a binding precedent of its precedential force.

The structural irony that Congress chose separate sessions precisely because the sessions were supportive (no revocation needed), yet the Constitution's text on the 24-hour convening requirement applies regardless of intent to revoke — used by CJ to argue that the review duty is independent of, and logically prior to, the revocation decision.

one_paragraph_summary: Panganiban analyzes the Hilbay group's June 6, 2017 mandamus petition (331 lawyers, 23 pages) seeking to compel Congress to convene in joint session to review Proclamation 216, after the Senate and House each passed separate supportive resolutions on May 31 without meeting jointly. He frames the constitutional question: Art. VII Sec. 18 says Congress 'voting jointly ... may revoke' ML, but the petitioners -- quoting the 1986 ConCom exchanges of delegates Bernas, Rodrigo, and Monsod (the last being both framer and current petitioner) -- argue that the Constitution requires joint deliberation as a reviewing duty independent of whether revocation is intended. Congress counters that joint session is required only to revoke, not to review. CJ finds the petitioners more persuasive on the text and framers' intent, and notes that Fortun vs Arroyo (2012) described Congress's joint-session duty as 'automatic' -- but argues that Fortun's pronouncements are mere obiter because GMA lifted ML before the Court could rule, stripping the language of precedential force. He recommends that the SC rule definitively on the joint-session requirement now for prospective guidance, but decline to issue a writ of mandamus compelling Congress -- extending the benefit of good faith given the Fortun ambiguity -- in order to uphold the rule of law for future ML scenarios.
